section.title: John's Ministry, the Baptism, and the Genealogy
section.sectionRationale: The infancy narratives close and the public story begins. Luke dates John's ministry by emperors and governors, then lets the forerunner preach a baptism of repentance and point beyond himself to the Mightier One. Jesus takes His place with sinners in the water, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks. Luke then traces the line back, not to Abraham only, but all the way to Adam, the son of God, framing Jesus as the second Adam for the whole human race.
section.thesis: The forerunner calls Israel to a repentance that bears fruit and points to the Coming One; and when Jesus stands with sinners in the Jordan, the Spirit descends and the Father names Him beloved Son, the last Adam who will succeed where the first fell.
section.frameNote: Five movements: John's prophetic call dated in world history; his preaching of repentance and its fruit; his witness to the Mightier One who baptizes with the Spirit and fire; the baptism of Jesus with the descending Spirit and the Father's voice; and the genealogy running back through David to Adam and to God.

units.label: John's prophetic call in history
units.note: the word of God comes in the wilderness

verses.text: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene,
during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness.
He went into all the region around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of {{metanoia|repentance}} for the forgiveness of sins,
as it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.
Every valley shall be filled in, and every mountain and hill made low. The crooked ways shall be made straight, and the rough ways smooth.
And all humanity will see God’s salvation.’”

units.label: A baptism of repentance and its fruit
units.note: produce fruit in keeping with repentance

verses.text: Then John said to the crowds coming out to be baptized by him, “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?

Produce fruit, then, in keeping with {{metanoia|repentance}}. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham.
The axe lies ready at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”
The crowds asked him, “What then should we do?”
John replied, “Whoever has two tunics should share with him who has none, and whoever has food should do the same.”
Even tax collectors came to be baptized. “Teacher,” they asked, “what should we do?”
“Collect no more than you are authorized,” he answered.
Then some soldiers asked him, “And what should we do?” “Do not take money by force or false accusation,” he said. “Be content with your wages.”

units.label: The One more powerful is coming
units.note: he will baptize with the Spirit and fire

verses.text: The people were waiting expectantly and were all wondering in their hearts if John could be the {{christos|Christ}}.

John answered all of them: “I {{baptizo|baptize}} you with water, but One more powerful than I will come, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.
His winnowing fork is in His hand to clear His threshing floor and to gather the wheat into His barn; but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”
With these and many other exhortations, John {{euangelizo|proclaimed the good news}} to the people.
But when he rebuked Herod the tetrarch regarding his brother’s wife Herodias and all the evils he had done,
Herod added this to them all: He locked John up in prison.
When all the people were being baptized, Jesus was baptized too. And as He was praying, heaven was opened,
and the Holy Spirit descended on Him in a bodily form like a dove. And a voice came from heaven: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.”

units.label: The genealogy to Adam and to God
units.note: son of Adam, son of God

verses.text: Jesus Himself was about thirty years old when He began His ministry. He was regarded as the son of Joseph, the son of Heli,
the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph,
the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai,
the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda,
the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri,
the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er,
the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi,
the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim,
the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David,
the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon,
the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah,
the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor,
the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah,
the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech,
the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalalel, the son of Cainan,
the son of Enosh, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.

metanoia.gloss: A change of mind that turns the whole life around; repentance. It is not mere regret but a reorientation away from sin toward God. John preaches a baptism of metanoia and insists it must show itself in fruit, in real changes of behavior toward the poor, in honest work, in contentment.

baptizo.gloss: To dip, immerse, or wash; to baptize. John baptizes with water as a sign of repentance, but he points to One who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire, an immersion in the very presence and purifying power of God that only the Messiah can give.

christos.gloss: The Anointed One, the Messiah, the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew Mashiach. The crowds wonder whether John himself might be the Christ; John firmly points away from himself to the Mightier One whose sandals he is unworthy to untie.

euangelizo.gloss: To announce good news, to proclaim glad tidings. Luke says that even John's stern call to repentance was gospel: it prepared the way for the salvation all humanity would see, so that the warning of judgment and the offer of mercy belong to one good announcement.

basic.context: After the birth stories, Luke opens the public history. He carefully dates John's ministry by the rulers of the day, then lets John preach in the wilderness. John calls the crowds to repent and to show it by changed lives, warns that heritage alone will not save them, and points beyond himself to a Mightier One. When Jesus is baptized, the Spirit comes down and the Father speaks. Luke then lists Jesus' ancestry all the way back to Adam and to God.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the dating in verses 1 and 2 as Luke's way of anchoring the gospel in real history: this happened under named emperors, governors, and priests. John's preaching is descriptive of his mission but also lays down an abiding pattern, real repentance bears fruit. The baptism scene is the hinge, where the Father, Son, and Spirit are all present. The genealogy is not filler; its final line, son of Adam, son of God, tells us who Jesus is.
basic.originalLanguages: John preaches metanoia, a repentance that turns the whole life around and shows in fruit. He baptizes with water, but points to One who will baptizo, immerse, people in the Holy Spirit and fire. The crowds wonder if John is the christos, the Anointed One; he points away from himself. And Luke calls even John's hard words euangelizo, good news, because they prepare the way for the salvation all will see.
basic.typology: John is the promised voice in the wilderness of Isaiah 40, preparing the Lord's way. The descending dove recalls the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation and the dove of Noah's new beginning. Above all, the genealogy back to Adam presents Jesus as the second Adam, the true Son who will stand where the first son of God fell.
basic.christ: Jesus, though sinless, steps into the water with sinners, identifying with the people He came to save. The Spirit rests on Him and the Father names Him beloved Son, echoing Psalm 2 and Isaiah 42, marking Him as King and Servant. As the son of Adam and Son of God, He is the new head of a renewed humanity.
basic.god: God speaks His word to an ordinary man in a desert, keeps His promise to send a forerunner, and reveals Himself as Father, Son, and Spirit at the Jordan. He is a God who judges fruitless trees yet offers a baptism of repentance and forgiveness, a God whose salvation all humanity will see.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 40:3-5 is the prophecy John fulfills. Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1 stand behind the Father's words. Acts 1:5 and 2:1-4 show the promised baptism with the Spirit poured out. Romans 5:12-19 and 1 Corinthians 15:45 unfold Jesus as the last Adam.
basic.oneStory: The long wait is ending. The forerunner prepares the way, the King steps into the water with sinners, and the Spirit and the Father mark Him out. By tracing the line to Adam, Luke shows that this is not merely Israel's story but the whole world's: the second Adam has come to undo the fall and to bring the salvation all humanity will see.

context.literary:
Luke 3 is the hinge between the infancy narratives and the public ministry, and its five movements are arranged with care. The chapter opens with a long, formal dating, then moves through John's preaching, John's exit from the stage, the baptism and the genealogy. Two things stand out. First, Luke removes John from the scene before Jesus is baptized. Verses 19 and 20 report that Herod locked John in prison, and only in verse 21 does Jesus come to the water. The order is not chronological, since John was still baptizing when Jesus came, but literary: the forerunner has finished his task and the stage is cleared for the One he announced.

Second, Luke's baptism of Jesus is almost an aside. The act is a subordinate clause, 'when all the people were being baptized, Jesus was baptized too,' and the weight falls on what follows, that He was praying, heaven was opened, the Spirit descended and the voice spoke. Prayer is a favorite Lukan marker of the great moments in Jesus' life, as in Luke 6:12, 9:18 and 9:28 and 29. Jesus is not simply submitting to a rite; He is praying at the threshold of His mission.

The preaching section is built on a triple repetition of the same question. The crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers each ask, 'What should we do?' in verses 10, 12 and 14, and John gives each a concrete answer. The question will be asked again at Pentecost, Acts 2:37. The scene lays a pattern: repentance must be specific, and each group is told to stop the particular sin of its own position.

The genealogy has a unique place. Matthew puts his at the start of his Gospel, but Luke places his between the Father's declaration of Sonship and the devil's challenge in Luke 4:3, 'If You are the Son of God.' The family tree is therefore an answer to the question of what kind of Son He is. Luke's list also runs backward, from Jesus to God, so the last words are the climax, 'the son of Adam, the son of God.'
context.historical:
Luke names seven political and religious figures to date John's call, and the details of each are secure. Tiberius became emperor in AD 14, so his fifteenth year falls around AD 28 or 29 by the usual count. Pontius Pilate governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36. Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea until AD 39, and his half-brother Philip ruled the territories to the north and east until AD 34. Lysanias, tetrarch of Abilene, is known from an inscription from that region that mentions a tetrarch of that name in the time of Tiberius. Annas had been high priest from about AD 6 to 15 and kept great influence, and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office from about AD 18 to 36, which is why the Gospels and Acts can speak of both together, as at Acts 4:6. The list is a deliberate catalogue of the powers of the day, and then it says that the word of God came not to any of them but to a man in the desert.

The wilderness around the Jordan was a thinly settled country, a place of retreat, testing and new beginnings in Israel's memory, and the Jordan itself was the river the people had crossed to enter the land. Ritual washing was an old practice in Judaism, and the community at Qumran, not far from where John worked, practiced repeated washings. John's baptism differs in that he baptizes people, once, as a sign of repentance and for the forgiveness of sins, verse 3. The Jewish historian Josephus mentions John and describes him as a good man who urged the Jews to virtue and baptism, and reports that Herod Antipas had him put to death.

The groups John addresses fit the social world of the Galilee and Perea. Tax collectors worked for the system of contracted collection and could enrich themselves by demanding more than was due, which is why John says 'Collect no more than you are authorized.' The soldiers were probably in the service of Antipas and were known to extort and to supplement a small wage. The generosity of two tunics shared is a simple matter of survival in a poor economy, and echoes the provision for the poor in the law, Leviticus 19:9 and 10.

Herod's imprisonment of John, which Luke mentions in verses 19 and 20, was over his marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife, and Mark 6:17 and 18 supplies the details. The genealogy then takes us back through the post-exilic names such as Zerubbabel and Shealtiel, verse 27, and on to the age of the kings.
context.canonical:
The chapter is anchored in Isaiah 40, which Luke quotes at greater length than the other Gospels. Matthew and Mark quote only the voice of Isaiah 40:3, but Luke continues through verse 5: every valley filled, every mountain made low, and 'all humanity will see God's salvation,' Luke 3:4 to 6. The final line is Luke's special point, since it ties John to the song of Simeon, who said his eyes had seen God's salvation, Luke 2:30. The opening of Isaiah 40, 'Comfort, comfort My people,' Isaiah 40:1, sets the whole scene as the end of exile.

John's warnings gather the language of the prophets. Fruit is the test of Israel's life in Isaiah's song of the vineyard, Isaiah 5:1 to 7, and the blessed person in Psalm 1 is a tree by streams while the wicked are chaff driven by wind, Psalm 1:3 and 4. The axe at the root and the unquenchable fire come from the prophets' announcements of the Day of the LORD, Malachi 4:1. The repentance of the heart that John demands is the old call to 'circumcise yourselves to the LORD,' Jeremiah 4:4. Jesus will later tell the parable of a fig tree given one more year, Luke 13:6 to 9, and teach that a tree is known by its fruit, Luke 6:43 to 45.

The baptism of Jesus joins several Scriptures at once. The words of the voice draw on Psalm 2:7, 'You are My Son,' and the Servant passage of Isaiah 42:1, 'in whom My soul delights,' and the choice of 'beloved' may recall the Father's description of Isaac in Genesis 22:2. The Spirit that descends fulfils Isaiah 11:2 and 61:1, which Jesus reads aloud in Nazareth, Luke 4:18, and which Peter later summarizes, 'God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power,' Acts 10:38. The promise of a baptism in the Spirit is repeated by the risen Lord at Acts 1:5.

The genealogy rests on the lists of Genesis 5, Genesis 11 and 1 Chronicles 1, 2 and 3, and it feeds Paul's reflections on Adam and Christ in Romans 5:12 to 19 and 1 Corinthians 15:45 to 49.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke writes so that his reader may know the certainty of what he has been taught, Luke 1:4, and he makes that point in this chapter by planting the gospel in recorded history. Seven named rulers make a date. A person who wanted to check what Luke claimed could ask about Tiberius, Pilate or Annas. The word of God, Luke says, came into a world that had real dates and real officials, and it still came to an obscure man at the margin.

He also wants his reader to hear John's preaching as a serious summons and not as picturesque background. Ancestry will not protect anyone, fruit must be visible, and judgment is near. Yet the sermon is not only threat. By the end of verse 18 Luke calls it good news. John tells people what to do, and the specificity of his answers shows that he expects real change in daily life: share, be honest, be content. Luke's hearers, who include comfortable and powerful people, are meant to feel the weight.

He means the baptism to show a Trinitarian revelation at the threshold of Jesus' mission: the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends and the Father speaks. Nothing in the account explains how this happened. Luke's concern is that the reader know that the One who is about to begin His work is publicly acknowledged and equipped from above.

The genealogy is Luke's last word on identity. By tracing the line to Adam and not stopping at Abraham or David, he shows Jesus as someone who belongs to the whole human family, and by closing with God he shows what kind of human He is. Readers are meant to carry the final phrase into the temptation that follows.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The details of John's ministry are descriptive. He was in the wilderness, he baptized in the Jordan, and he said what he said to those particular audiences. The church does not take from this that every believer must go to the desert or that baptism must always occur in a river. Nor does it take that every tax collector or soldier must change jobs, since John does not tell them to leave their occupations but to do them honestly. What persists is the principle that real repentance changes the way a person behaves in the place where they are.

John's specific commands, however, show what fruit looks like. Sharing a second coat, giving food to those who have none, refusing to cheat, and being content with one's wages are described as the outworking of repentance. They are the kind of instruction the New Testament repeats, as in 1 John 3:17 and Ephesians 4:28. The principle is generous, and the examples show the form it takes.

The baptism of Jesus is a unique event and not a pattern to be copied in its details. Believers are not anointed by the Spirit in the same way for the same office, nor do they hear the Father's voice from the heavens. What can be said is that the believer is united to the One who was named beloved Son, so that the Spirit now bears witness that we are children of God, Romans 8:15 and 16. The genealogy is likewise a statement of who He is, not a model of how every believer should trace descent.

debates.question: Why was the sinless Jesus baptized?

views.label: To stand with sinners
views.case: John's baptism was for the forgiveness of sins, and Jesus had none to confess. He receives it as the Representative of the people He came to save, as Isaiah says of the Servant that He would be numbered with the transgressors, Isaiah 53:12, which Jesus applies to Himself in Luke 22:37. The baptism is the first step of the road that ends at the cross, where He is made sin on our behalf, 2 Corinthians 5:21.

views.label: To fulfil all righteousness and be anointed
views.case: Matthew records Jesus telling John it is fitting to fulfil all righteousness, Matthew 3:15. On this reading the baptism is an act of obedience to the Father and the occasion of the Spirit's anointing for His work, as Peter says in Acts 10:38. It marks the start of His public ministry.

views.label: The approval of John's mission
views.case: Others stress that Jesus' baptism publicly endorses John's call to repentance, and with it the whole preparation of Israel. The Gospel of John adds that John's purpose in baptizing was so that Jesus might be revealed to Israel, John 1:31.

debates.bearing: These readings overlap more than they conflict. All agree that Jesus does not repent of personal sin, and that He enters the water as the Obedient One for the sake of others. Luke himself has Jesus later speak of a baptism He must undergo, Luke 12:50, which is a way of saying that the Jordan points toward the cross.

debates.question: Why does Luke's genealogy differ from Matthew's?

views.label: Luke gives Mary's line
views.case: Matthew has Joseph's father as Jacob, Matthew 1:16, while Luke has Heli, Luke 3:23, and Luke's list goes through David's son Nathan, 2 Samuel 5:14, where Matthew goes through Solomon. Some take Luke to be tracing Mary's ancestry, with 'son of Heli' meaning son-in-law, so that both parents descend from David. Luke's careful wording that Jesus was 'regarded as' the son of Joseph supports an emphasis on the human line other than Joseph's.

views.label: Luke gives Joseph's line by another route
views.case: An old explanation holds that both lists belong to Joseph, one by legal descent and one by biological descent, the difference arising from a levirate marriage in which one man fathered a child in another man's name. Both lists share Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, Luke 3:27 and Matthew 1:12, which shows that the two lines cross.

views.label: Two lists with two purposes
views.case: Others emphasize that ancient genealogies served theological aims and need not be complete. Matthew shapes his into three sets of fourteen to show Jesus as son of David and Abraham, and Luke runs his back to Adam to show a Savior for all humanity, so that the differences are part of the message and not a flaw.

debates.bearing: No explanation is certain, and the sources do not allow us to settle every name. What is clear is that both Gospels insist on the Davidic descent of Jesus, and Luke's distinctive contribution is the final phrase, which sets Jesus at the head of the human family and places Him as God's Son.

debates.question: What is the baptism 'with the Holy Spirit and with fire'?

views.label: One baptism of judgment
views.case: The context in verse 17 is the winnowing of the threshing floor, with unquenchable fire for the chaff. On this reading the Spirit and fire together describe the coming judgment through which the Messiah separates the wheat from the chaff.

views.label: One baptism of cleansing
views.case: Fire is also a prophetic image of refining, as in Malachi 3:2 and 3 and Isaiah 4:4. The Spirit and fire together may describe a purifying work that burns away what is impure, which fits the tongues like fire that rested on each believer at Pentecost, Acts 2:3.

views.label: One baptism with two outcomes
views.case: The Greek places both nouns under a single preposition, so that one baptism meets two responses: those who receive the Messiah are filled and refined, and those who refuse are consumed. The same fire that purifies gold destroys chaff.

debates.bearing: Luke has the Spirit and the fire fall at Pentecost, where the Spirit is given and the fire sits on the disciples, and the language of final judgment awaits the day of the Lord. The third reading respects both and keeps verses 16 and 17 together as one announcement.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke opens with a formula that his readers would recognize, 'the word of God came to John,' using rhema, a word for a spoken utterance. The same construction in the Septuagint introduces the call of the prophets, as in Jeremiah 1:1 to 2 and Hosea 1:1. The long list of rulers sits on one side of the sentence and the word of God on the other. John is being introduced not as a reformer but as a prophet in the line of Jeremiah and Hosea, after centuries of silence.

In verse 7 John calls the crowd gennemata echidnon, a 'brood of vipers,' with a noun meaning offspring. The word for the snake's young recalls the question of descent, which is exactly what verse 8 takes up. They want to be 'children of Abraham,' and John says they are the offspring of vipers. The reply plays on a pair of Hebrew words that sound alike, banim, 'sons,' and avanim, 'stones.' God could raise sons from stones as easily as from Abraham's line. The point is that membership in the covenant was never a matter of biology alone.

The 'fruit in keeping with repentance' of verse 8 uses axios, 'worthy of' or 'weighing as much as,' so that the fruit must match the repentance, and the verb of verse 9, keitai, 'lies' or 'is set,' says the axe is already laid at the root. The same verb described the child in Luke 2:34, 'appointed' for the fall and rise of many, an echo of Luke's own wording that may be coincidental.

The soldiers' advice in verse 14 uses two verbs that name the abuses of their position. The first, diaseio, means to shake violently, so to extort by threat. The second, sykophanteo, means to accuse falsely for profit, and it is the verb Zacchaeus uses when he confesses that if he has cheated anyone he will repay four times as much, Luke 19:8. The wages, opsonia, were originally the rations of a soldier, and the command to be content is directed at the particular temptation of men with power and low pay.

In verse 16 the clause 'He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire' uses a single en, 'in,' before both nouns, so that one immersion is in view. The word in verse 17 for 'unquenchable,' asbestos, literally means that which cannot be put out. John also speaks of the winnowing fork, ptyon, and the threshing floor, halon, which are the tools of the harvest and which come at the end of the agricultural year, a natural picture of separation.

In verse 22 the Spirit descends 'in a bodily form,' somatiko eidei, a phrase peculiar to Luke, so that the descent is something visible and not only an inner experience. The Father's words begin 'You are My beloved Son,' and the adjective agapetos, 'beloved,' is the word the Greek Old Testament uses of Isaac in Genesis 22:2, the son whom Abraham was told to offer. The verb eudokeo, 'I am well pleased,' comes from the same family as the noun eudokia that the angels sang in Luke 2:14, so that the 'favor' announced over the shepherds' field now rests on a named Person. Some manuscripts, notably Codex Bezae, replace the second half with the words of Psalm 2:7, 'today I have begotten You,' which most scholars take to be a later change, since the better witnesses agree with the text given here.

Verse 23 says Jesus was 'regarded as' the son of Joseph, using the imperfect of nomizo, 'it was supposed,' a quiet signal that the supposition was not the whole truth, in line with the account of the virgin conception, Luke 1:34 and 35. The list runs through a series of genitives, each 'of so-and-so,' until the last, 'tou theou,' 'of God.' The Septuagint's Genesis 11:12 has a Cainan between Arphaxad and Shelah that is absent from the Hebrew text, and Luke's list in verse 36 agrees with the Greek version.

typology.fulfillment: Paul says Adam is 'a pattern of the One to come,' Romans 5:14. Luke ends the genealogy with Adam, 'the son of God,' and then follows it at once with the voice at the Jordan, 'You are My beloved Son,' and the temptation, 'If You are the Son of God,' Luke 4:3. Adam was a son placed in a garden and failed at the first question. Jesus is a Son placed in a wilderness and succeeds at all three. Paul calls Him the last Adam and the second man, 1 Corinthians 15:45 to 47. The pattern falls short in that Adam's failure was passed to his descendants, while Christ's obedience is credited to His, Romans 5:19.

typology.type: Israel's passage through the water and the wilderness
typology.fulfillment: Israel came through the sea, were 'baptized into Moses,' 1 Corinthians 10:1 and 2, and then spent forty years in the wilderness being tested, Deuteronomy 8:2 and 3. Jesus is named Son at the water and is led by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days, Luke 4:1 and 2, answering each temptation from Deuteronomy. The correspondence casts Him as the true Israel, the Son who does what Israel did not. The type is limited because Israel's testing was for failure and Jesus' is for success, and He does not fail for a single day.

God called Isaac 'your son, your only son, whom you love,' Genesis 22:2, and Abraham took him up the mountain to be offered. The Father's address to Jesus at the Jordan uses the same word for beloved. The correspondence is of a beloved son given over to sacrifice, and Paul takes up its fulfillment in the line that God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The shape is the same, and what differs is that Isaac was spared at the last moment by a ram provided, while Jesus was not spared, since He is the provided Lamb, John 1:29.

typology.type: The Elijah who prepares the way
typology.fulfillment: Malachi promised that God would send Elijah the prophet before the great Day of the LORD to turn hearts, Malachi 4:5 and 6. John goes before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, as Gabriel said, Luke 1:17, and Jesus calls him the Elijah who was to come, Matthew 11:14. The correspondence is of role and message, and John does not claim to be Elijah in person, John 1:21. The type is fulfilled in that the hearts John turned prepared people for the Lord, and it falls short only in that the prophet's mission is to point away from himself, John 3:30.

In the first creation the Spirit of God hovered over the waters, Genesis 1:2, and after the flood a dove brought an olive leaf to show that the waters had receded, Genesis 8:11. Neither text says that a dove is a sign of the Spirit, and the New Testament does not draw the link explicitly, so this is a suggestive echo and not a settled type. Yet the Gospel scene has the same elements, water, the Spirit and a new beginning. Luke has the Spirit rest on the One through whom the world is made new, and the echo is that a new creation starts at the Jordan.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ by showing Him at the point where He stands with sinners and is also set apart from them. He comes among a crowd of people being baptized for forgiveness, and He is baptized too. Hebrews says He was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin, Hebrews 4:15, and Paul says that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, 2 Corinthians 5:21. The Jordan is therefore the first public step of a road that ends at the cross. Jesus Himself draws the line when He says, 'I have a baptism to undergo, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished,' Luke 12:50. The water at the beginning anticipates the death at the end.

It leads to Christ by the Spirit. John says the One who follows will baptize in the Spirit and fire, and the passage shows the Spirit descending on Him first. Jesus is the Anointed One in the strict sense of the word, the Christ, and Luke will show Him claiming Isaiah 61:1 at Nazareth, 'The Spirit of the Lord is on Me,' Luke 4:18, and Peter summarizes it, 'God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power,' Acts 10:38. He is not only anointed. He is also the One who gives the Spirit to others, as John the Evangelist says, 'He is the One who baptizes with the Holy Spirit,' John 1:33, and as the risen Lord promises in Acts 1:5.

It leads to Christ by the Father's words. 'You are My beloved Son' is the language of Psalm 2, the enthronement of the Davidic king, and 'in You I am well pleased' draws on the Servant of the LORD in Isaiah 42:1. The two figures, king and servant, are fused in one voice. The same Son who will reign is the One who will serve and suffer, which becomes the shape of the Gospel, as in Luke 22:27 and 24:26.

It leads to Christ by the genealogy. He is the son of David, so the promise of an everlasting throne rests on Him, Luke 1:32 and 33. He is the son of Abraham, so all nations are blessed in Him, Genesis 22:18. And He is the son of Adam, so He enters the human story as one of us. Where the first Adam fell, the last Adam stands. Paul can then say that as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive, 1 Corinthians 15:22.

The passage also shows John's relation to Him. John says he is not worthy to untie the sandals, and the fourth Gospel adds that Jesus existed before him, John 1:15, and that He must increase while John decreases, John 3:30.

A caution is needed. The dove, the water and the numbers of generations should not be turned into hidden codes. What Luke makes clear is the identity and mission of Jesus: He is Son, Spirit-bearer, Servant and Adam. The Gospel then goes on to show how He lives out each of these.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who speaks into history through those who are not at its centre. The powers of the day are named one by one, from the emperor to the high priests, and then the word of God comes to the son of a village priest in the wilderness. God does not wait for palaces or temples. He sends His word to whom He will, and what He says carries more weight than all the officials listed. The doctrine of God that follows is that He is sovereign over the political order and free to choose the lowly to speak for Him, as Isaiah's own prophecy of a voice in the wilderness had implied.

It shows a God who is both just and merciful, and whose justice is real. John speaks of coming wrath, an axe at the root and a fire that cannot be put out, and in the same sermon he preaches forgiveness of sins and the revelation of salvation to all humanity. The two aspects are not in conflict. The God who will judge is the same God who has prepared a way of escape, and the call to repent is itself a mercy because it comes before the judgment. Repentance is described as urgent not because God is eager to condemn but because the day is near.

It shows a God who is not bound by lineage. 'God can raise up children for Abraham out of these stones,' and so the claim of ancestry is empty. God's freedom to make a people out of nothing is a recurrent theme of Scripture, as in Isaiah 51:1 and 2, which calls Israel to look to the rock from which they were cut and to Abraham their father, one man whom God called and blessed and made many. Grace is not something that can be inherited.

It shows a God who is Trinity. At the Jordan the Father speaks from heaven, the Spirit descends and the Son stands in the water in prayer. The text does not argue the doctrine. It simply shows three distinct Persons acting together at one time, and it remains one of the clearest places where the Gospel makes the doctrine visible. It also shows the love within God, since the Father speaks of the Son as beloved and as the object of His delight.

It shows a God who is faithful across the generations. The long list of names from Jesus back to Adam, from the exile through the kings to the patriarchs, covers the whole of human history and says that none of it was outside His purpose. The same God who made the first man is the God who sends the last Adam.

For worship, the passage teaches awe at the Father's affirmation and gratitude for the way Jesus took His place among those who needed forgiveness. It also teaches that worship is not complete without obedience. The crowd's question, 'What should we do?' is the right reaction to hearing God's word, and the answer is a life that bears fruit.

crossReferences.note: The prophet announces comfort for Jerusalem, a voice calling in the wilderness, a highway for God, and the revelation of His glory to all flesh. Luke quotes verses 3 to 5 and applies them to John. The longer quotation allows him to end on the promise that all humanity will see God's salvation, which echoes Simeon in Luke 2:30.

God promises to send a messenger to prepare the way before Him, and then the Lord will suddenly come to His temple. Luke's mention of the messenger in Luke 1:76 and 3:4 draws on this, and Jesus says of John, 'This is the one about whom it is written,' Luke 7:27. The forerunner and the Lord come in the order Malachi gave.

The song of the vineyard describes a beloved who dug, planted and waited for good grapes but found sour ones, and so removed the hedge. John's picture of fruitless trees and the axe stands in the same tradition. God expects fruit from those He has planted, and Jesus uses the image again in Luke 13:6 to 9.

The righteous are like a tree planted by streams, yielding fruit in season, and the wicked are like chaff blown away by the wind. John's tree and chaff pair these two images in a single message. His winnowing fork separates wheat from chaff, so the destination of the two is as the psalm describes.

The LORD declares to His anointed King, 'You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.' The Father's voice at the Jordan begins with the same words. The Psalm's picture of the enthroned king is therefore tied to the Spirit-anointed Jesus, and the later verses of the psalm, which promise Him the nations, explain the mission that begins here.

The LORD presents His chosen Servant, in whom His soul delights, and puts His Spirit on Him so that He will bring justice to the nations in gentleness. The Father's pleasure in the Son and the descent of the Spirit match these lines, and so the Jordan is the moment when the Servant is publicly identified.

God tells Abraham to take his son, his only son whom he loves, and offer him on the mountain of Moriah. The description of Isaac as the beloved son may sit behind the Father's words at the Jordan. If so, the baptism already hints that this beloved Son will be given up, a link Paul makes explicit in Romans 8:32.

The risen Jesus tells the disciples that John baptized with water but that in a few days they will be baptized with the Holy Spirit. This is the fulfillment of John's promise in Luke 3:16. The Spirit that came on Jesus at the Jordan comes on His people at Pentecost, so the One who received the Spirit is the One who gives Him.

Paul sets the one man Adam, through whom sin and death entered the world, against the one man Jesus Christ, through whom grace and righteousness abound. Luke's genealogy places Jesus at the end of the line of Adam, and Paul explains why that matters: He undoes what Adam did for all who are in Him.

The first man Adam became a living being, and the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. Paul says the man of dust and the man from heaven fix two kinds of humanity. Luke's genealogy shows Jesus belongs to the line of the first, and the Jordan shows Him as the head of the second.

Jesus says that He has come to ignite a fire and that He has a baptism to undergo, and how distressed He is until it is accomplished. The baptism and the fire of Luke 3:16 are taken up here in His own words, and the baptism He must undergo is His death. The Jordan points forward to the cross.

Matthew's genealogy begins with Abraham and descends through the kings of Judah, in three sets of fourteen, to Jesus the Messiah. Setting it beside Luke's shows two portraits of the same person. Matthew presents the royal and covenant heir for Israel, and Luke presents the Savior who belongs to the whole human race.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with God making a man in His own likeness and calling him His son, and Luke ends his genealogy on that point, 'the son of Adam, the son of God.' The list covers the whole story in miniature: Adam and Seth, Noah and the flood, Abraham and the covenant, David and the throne, and the exile and return under Zerubbabel. Every name stands for a chapter in the long account of God's patience. By running the list backward from Jesus, Luke shows that the entire history leads up to Him.

The passage answers the question of what has become of the promises. John's call, in the dated reign of a Roman emperor, shows that after centuries of silence the word of God has come again, and that Isaiah's promise of a voice in the wilderness and of comfort after exile is being kept. John's warnings answer another question, why Israel remained in distress despite the covenant: fruit was lacking, and heritage was not enough. The vineyard song and the prophets' warnings had said so, and now the final call has come.

It also sets up the story's next movement. The Spirit-filled Son goes at once into the wilderness, Luke 4:1, to face the tempter as Adam and Israel had faced him, and to begin the work that will lead to a cross. The promised baptism of the Spirit will be given at Pentecost, and the message of repentance and forgiveness will be preached to all nations beginning from Jerusalem, Luke 24:47. The genealogy's reach to Adam foreshadows the mission to the Gentiles that will fill Acts.

The Jordan scene is also the moment when the creation, fall and redemption of the Bible touch each other. The Son stands in the water, the Spirit hovers as at the beginning, and the Father speaks as at the first creation, and a new humanity begins in the One who is the last Adam. His obedience will overturn the disobedience at the start of the story, as Paul says, Romans 5:19.

The new creation is the end of the passage's hopes. Isaiah's promise that all humanity will see God's salvation is realized in the multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language that stands before the throne and the Lamb, Revelation 7:9 and 10. The river of the water of life flows from the throne, the tree of life is open again, and there is no longer any curse, Revelation 22:1 to 3. The genealogy that began with the man driven out of the garden ends with a family restored to God's presence, who will see His face.

sermon.title: The Baptism of Jesus
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Luke, this message on Luke 3:21 explains why the sinless Jesus was baptized, how His baptism identified Him with the sinners He came to save, and how it inaugurated His public ministry as the Spirit-anointed, beloved Son. A faithful, expository handling of the climax of this movement.

quiz.q: What did John call the crowds to do?

options.text: To repent and produce fruit in keeping with repentance, not resting on their descent from Abraham.
options.note: This is exactly John's message: a baptism of repentance that shows itself in changed lives, verses 8 to 14.

options.text: To be baptized as an outward sign of turning to God.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but John insists the sign must be matched by real fruit, so this is only part of the picture.

options.text: To claim Abraham as their father and so be safe from wrath.
options.note: This is the very presumption John warns against; heritage without repentance cannot save.

options.text: To take up arms against Rome and Herod.
options.note: John never calls for revolt; he tells even soldiers to be content and just.

quiz.q: How did John describe the One who was coming after him?

options.text: As One more powerful, whose sandals John was unworthy to untie, who would baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire.
options.note: This is John's own testimony in verse 16, pointing away from himself to the Mightier One.

options.text: As a great prophet in the line of Elijah.
options.note: The Coming One is greater than any prophet; this understates who He is, though it moves in the right direction.

options.text: As a political liberator who would overthrow Herod.
options.note: A misplaced, worldly expectation; John speaks of a baptism with the Spirit and fire, not a coup.

options.text: As no one greater than himself, since John was the Christ.
options.note: John flatly denies being the Christ and points to the One mightier than he.

quiz.q: What happened when Jesus was baptized?

options.text: Heaven opened, the Spirit descended like a dove, and the Father's voice named Him His beloved Son.
options.note: Verses 21 and 22 reveal the Father, Son, and Spirit together at the Jordan.

options.text: Jesus identified with sinners by taking His place in the water.
options.note: True and important, but it names the meaning of His act rather than the full event Luke records.

options.text: It was an ordinary baptism with nothing to set it apart.
options.note: This misses the descending Spirit and the Father's voice that mark this baptism as unique.

options.text: Jesus was baptized to be cleansed from His own sin.
options.note: Jesus is sinless; His baptism is solidarity and obedience, not personal cleansing.

quiz.q: Why does Luke trace Jesus' genealogy back to Adam, the son of God?

options.text: To present Jesus as the second Adam and Savior of all humanity, not of Israel only.
options.note: The closing line, son of Adam, son of God, frames Jesus as the new head of the human race.

options.text: To establish Jesus' legal descent through Joseph.
options.note: Luke does trace the line through Joseph, but the deeper aim is the reach back to Adam and God.

options.text: To show Jesus was descended only from David.
options.note: David is in the list, but Luke goes far beyond him to Adam; limiting it to David misses the point.

options.text: To suggest Jesus was just one more ordinary link in a human chain.
options.note: The opposite: the genealogy exalts Jesus as the Son of God and the new Adam.

quiz.q: What does John's image of the axe at the root of the trees teach?

options.text: That God looks for real fruit, and repentance that produces none faces judgment.
options.note: Verse 9 warns that every fruitless tree is cut down; repentance must be genuine.

options.text: That doing enough good works will earn God's acceptance.
options.note: Fruit matters, but it flows from true repentance rather than earning God's favor; this half-truth misplaces the emphasis.

options.text: That religious heritage will shelter us from judgment.
options.note: This is precisely what John denies when he says God can raise up children for Abraham from stones.

options.text: That God never actually judges anyone.
options.note: The image is a clear warning of real judgment on fruitlessness.

questions: John tied real repentance to real fruit, sharing clothes and food, honest work, contentment. Where might genuine repentance be asking for visible change in your everyday life?
The crowds trusted their descent from Abraham. What heritage, reputation, or past experience are you tempted to rest in instead of ongoing repentance and faith?
Jesus, though sinless, stepped into the water alongside sinners. How does it move you that your Savior was willing to stand in your place from the very start?
At the Jordan the Father said, 'You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.' How would it change your day to live as one loved by God in His beloved Son?
Luke calls even John's hard words good news, because they prepared the way for salvation. Where is God using a hard word to prepare a way of grace in your life right now?

translationNotes.note: All humanity will see God's salvation renders literally all flesh will see the salvation of God, quoting Isaiah 40:3-5 in the Greek Septuagint. Luke extends the Isaiah citation further than Matthew or Mark to stress that salvation reaches beyond Israel to all people.

Baptize you with water and with the Holy Spirit and with fire can also be rendered in water and in the Holy Spirit and in fire, as the BSB footnote notes. The fire suggests both purifying and judgment, gathered up in the winnowing image of verse 17.

You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased draws on Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1. A few Western witnesses, such as Codex Bezae, read the fuller words of Psalm 2:7, You are My Son, today I have begotten You; the BSB follows the widely attested reading.

Luke's genealogy ascends from Joseph to Adam and God, differing from Matthew's descending list from Abraham. Verse 23 says Jesus was regarded as the son of Joseph, guarding the virgin birth already told in chapters 1 and 2, and many take Luke's line to trace Jesus' ancestry in a distinct way from Matthew's royal line.
